I have been doing this for nineteen years and I can tell you where the money goes. It goes to courses, and courses are the least effective development there is, and everybody in this room already knows that. What actually moves somebody is a job that is slightly too big for them, with somebody watching. That is it. That is the whole science. A stretch assignment costs nothing and works, and a course costs four thousand dollars and produces a certificate. So why do we keep buying courses? Because a course is easy to approve and a stretch assignment requires a manager to accept some risk on their own numbers. Nobody wants to be the manager whose project went wrong because they gave it to somebody who was not quite ready. Until we solve that, we will keep spending the budget on rooms with slides in them.

I have been running plants for twelve years and I got the first one because somebody took a risk that, honestly, I would probably not take today. I had been a supervisor for two years. Two. There were people on that site who had been there longer than I had been alive, and I was going to tell them how to run a shift. What made it work was not me. It was that my director told me, in front of nobody, that he expected me to get about a third of it wrong and that his job was to catch the third that mattered. He had been doing this long enough to know which third that was. And he checked in every Friday for six months, twenty minutes, never longer. I have given three people that same jump since then, and I have not always got it right, but not once has the problem been that they were not ready. It has been that I was not watching.
